title: MODULE 03 — CSS Engineering and Modern Layout Systems

overview.text: This module moves students from writing basic CSS declarations to engineering complete, responsive, maintainable user interfaces.
After learning HTML document structure and semantic elements in Module 02, students will now learn how to control the appearance, layout, positioning, behavior, and responsiveness of those elements.

The focus is not simply making websites look attractive. It is understanding how browsers calculate styles, how layout algorithms work, how complex interfaces are structured, and how to build consistent design systems that can scale across large applications.
Move beyond basic styling and learn how to engineer complex interfaces.

CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) is the language used to describe the presentation of HTML documents. It controls the appearance, layout, positioning, typography, spacing, animations, and responsive behavior of web interfaces.

Professional frontend engineering requires much more than writing individual CSS properties. Developers must understand the cascade, specificity, inheritance, layout algorithms, the box model, stacking contexts, responsive sizing, typography, animation, and scalable styling architecture.
This module develops the ability to design and implement production-quality interfaces using modern CSS techniques.
By the end of this module, students should be able to:

items: Understand CSS syntax, selectors, declarations, and the cascade.
Analyze CSS specificity and inheritance to resolve styling conflicts.
Understand the box model and accurately calculate element dimensions.
Control document flow using display, position, overflow, and stacking contexts.
Build flexible one-dimensional layouts using Flexbox.
Design complex two-dimensional layouts using CSS Grid.
Use responsive units, CSS mathematical functions, and custom properties.
Apply typography, font systems, visual hierarchy, and text layout principles.
Use pseudo-classes, pseudo-elements, combinators, and advanced selectors.
Build transitions, transforms, and keyframe animations.
Organize CSS using scalable architecture and naming conventions.
Implement component-level styling using CSS Modules.
Design responsive interfaces for desktop, tablet, and mobile devices.
Debug layout and styling problems using browser developer tools.

sections.title: LESSON 01 — CSS Syntax, Selectors and Cascade

blocks.text: CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets.
It is a stylesheet language used to describe how HTML documents should be displayed.
HTML defines the document's structure and meaning, while CSS determines how that structure is visually presented.
Without additional styling, the browser applies its default styles.
We can change the appearance using CSS:
The browser interprets the CSS and applies the relevant styles to the matching HTML elements.
A CSS rule consists of a selector and a declaration block.
Identifies the HTML elements to which the rule applies.
Contains the declarations that define the styles.
A property identifies which aspect of an element is being controlled.
A value defines the setting for a property.
A property-value pair followed by a semicolon.
A declaration block may contain multiple declarations.
Comments allow developers to document their stylesheets.
Comments are ignored by the CSS styling process.
Use them to clarify complex implementation decisions rather than documenting every obvious declaration.
1.4 Ways to Add CSS to HTML
There are three traditional ways to apply CSS.
Styles are written directly inside an HTML element using the `style` attribute.

blocks.text: Inline CSS should generally not be the primary styling strategy for a production application.
Styles are written inside a `style` element in the HTML document.
This can be useful for small standalone documents and demonstrations.
Styles are stored in a separate stylesheet.
External stylesheets are generally preferable for maintainable projects because they separate document structure from presentation and allow styles to be shared across pages.
Selectors determine which elements receive particular styles.
CSS provides different selector categories for targeting elements.
The universal selector matches all elements.
It is frequently used for consistent box-sizing behavior.
Targets elements by their HTML tag name.
Targets elements with a particular class.
A class can be shared by multiple elements.
Targets an element with a particular ID.
IDs should be unique within the document.
In large applications, class selectors are generally easier to reuse and maintain than ID selectors for styling.
Attribute selectors are useful when styling elements based on their configuration or state-related attributes.
A space targets matching elements located anywhere inside another element.
Targets paragraphs inside course cards, including nested descendants.
This targets only `h2` elements that are direct children of `.course-card`.
The `+` operator targets the immediately following sibling.
The `~` operator targets matching following siblings.
This applies to matching paragraphs that follow the heading within the same parent element.
Multiple selectors can share the same declarations.
However, selectors should be grouped only when they genuinely need the same styling.
The cascade is the process browsers use to determine which CSS declarations apply when multiple declarations compete.
This explains why the last CSS declaration does not always win.
Both selectors have equivalent specificity, origin, and layer placement.
The second declaration wins because it appears later in the applicable stylesheet order.
The ID selector has greater specificity than the type selector.
Therefore, the text becomes red even though the paragraph selector appears earlier or later in the stylesheet.
Modern CSS supports cascade layers through `@layer`.
They allow developers to establish a predictable order among groups of stylesheet rules.
Cascade layers are useful when applications contain many stylesheets or third-party libraries.
For normal declarations within the same origin, later layers take precedence over earlier layers before specificity is compared.
Important declarations have a different layer-order behavior, so layer precedence must be understood alongside `!important`.
A project may separate its styles into files.

styles/

These stylesheets can be included through HTML or imported through a build system.
For production applications, the build system often manages stylesheet imports and bundling.
Browsers apply their own default styles to HTML elements.
For example, browsers commonly assign default margins to headings and paragraphs.
A CSS reset establishes a more predictable baseline.
A reset should remove unnecessary browser inconsistencies without accidentally removing useful native behavior.
A normalization stylesheet instead aims to preserve useful defaults while making browser behavior more consistent.

sections.title: LESSON 02 — Specificity, Inheritance and the Box Model

blocks.text: Specificity is one of the mechanisms browsers use to decide which declaration wins when competing CSS rules have the same relevant cascade precedence.
The text becomes red because the ID selector has greater specificity than the class and type selectors.
Specificity is conceptually represented using four components:
The values are compared lexicographically rather than added as ordinary numbers.
For example, two ID selectors outweigh any number of class selectors for specificity comparison.
An inline style generally has higher specificity than ordinary author stylesheet selectors, but it is not an absolute override against every possible cascade condition.
The `!important` flag changes importance precedence and should not be treated as another ordinary specificity point.
2.3 Why Excessive Specificity Is a Problem
This selector is difficult to override.
Good CSS architecture generally favors predictable, relatively low-specificity selectors.
This makes styles easier to reuse, test, and change.
The `!important` flag gives a declaration important priority within the relevant cascade origin and layer rules.
Even a more specific ordinary declaration will not normally override this important declaration at the same applicable origin and layer precedence.
However, other important declarations and cascade origins may still take precedence.
Overusing `!important` creates difficult stylesheets because normal cascade relationships become harder to understand.
Use it sparingly and for justified cases, such as certain utility classes or unavoidable third-party overrides.
Inheritance allows certain CSS properties to pass from parent elements to their descendants.
Descendant elements normally inherit the text color and font family unless another applicable declaration overrides them.
Many layout and box properties are not inherited.
Inheritance behavior depends on each property's definition.
CSS provides several special global values.

sections.title: LESSON 03 — Display, Positioning and Stacking Contexts

blocks.text: The `display` property determines how an element participates in layout.
It controls the element's outer and inner display behavior.
A block-level box generally participates in normal flow by starting on a new line and extending across the available inline space of its containing block by default.
Examples of common block elements include:
Block boxes can generally have explicit width, height, padding, and margin.
Inline boxes participate within a line of text.
Inline elements generally flow with surrounding text.
Width and height do not normally control their inline dimensions in the same way they do for block boxes.
Vertical margins and padding on inline boxes also have special layout behavior.
`inline-block` combines characteristics of inline and block-level layout.
It allows an element to participate inline while supporting a more box-like dimension model.
The `display: none` declaration removes an element and its descendants from the rendered layout.
The content remains represented in the DOM but does not generate its normal rendered boxes.
With `visibility: hidden`, the element generally retains its layout space while remaining invisible.
The `opacity: 0` approach makes an element transparent but does not remove it from layout or automatically disable its interaction.
The `flow-root` display value establishes a new block formatting context.
It can help contain floats and create a separate block formatting context without using older clearfix techniques.
The `position` property controls how an element is placed within the layout.
Static is the default positioning behavior.
The element participates in normal document flow.
The `top`, `right`, `bottom`, and `left` offsets do not position an ordinarily static element.
Relative positioning keeps an element in normal flow while allowing its rendered box to be visually offset.
The original space occupied by the element is generally preserved.
Relative positioning is also commonly used to establish a containing block for absolutely positioned descendants.
Absolute positioning removes an element from normal document flow and positions it relative to its applicable containing block.
The badge is positioned relative to the course card because the card establishes its containing block.
Do not use absolute positioning as the primary layout system for an entire page.
Fixed positioning places an element relative to its fixed-positioning containing block, commonly the viewport.
Some ancestor properties, such as transforms, can change the containing block behavior of fixed descendants.
Sticky positioning behaves like relative positioning until the relevant scroll threshold is reached, after which the element sticks within its containing scrollport and containing block constraints.
A sticky element requires an appropriate inset value and a suitable scroll container.
Overflow and parent sizing can affect where and whether sticky positioning works as expected.
The `z-index` property controls stack ordering within the applicable stacking context.
A larger number does not guarantee that an element appears above every other element on the page.
Stacking contexts create independent stacking environments.
A stacking context is a self-contained visual stacking group.
Certain CSS conditions create stacking contexts.

A containing block establishes the coordinate system used for certain positioned elements and percentage-based layout calculations.
The child uses the parent's padding-box-related containing block rules for absolute positioning.
Containing blocks can also be established by certain properties beyond positioning, including transforms and filters in relevant situations.

Flexbox, or the Flexible Box Layout Module, is a CSS layout system designed primarily for one-dimensional layouts.
It helps distribute available space and align elements along a row or column.

4.3 Understanding the Main Axis and Cross Axis
The main axis is determined by `flex-direction`.
This distinction is important because `justify-content` aligns along the main axis, while `align-items` aligns along the cross axis.
The `flex-direction` property determines the direction in which items are arranged.
Places items along the main inline axis, which is horizontal in the usual horizontal writing mode.
Places items vertically in the usual horizontal writing mode.
Remember that reverse directions can affect visual order without changing the underlying DOM or reading order.
Avoid using them to correct an incorrectly structured document.
`justify-content` distributes items along the main axis.
Items are placed toward the start of the main axis.
Items are centered along the main axis.
Items are placed toward the end.
Distributes equal spacing between items and the container edges.
`align-items` aligns flex items along the cross axis.
This is a common way to vertically align navigation content.
Modern logical alignment terminology such as `start` and `end` can also be used where supported by the relevant alignment property.
`align-content` controls the distribution of multiple flex lines along the cross axis.

items: There is additional cross-axis space to distribute.

blocks.text: `align-items` aligns items within their respective flex lines, while `align-content` distributes the lines themselves.
By default, flex items are generally arranged on a single line.
`flex-wrap` allows them to move onto additional lines.
Wrapping is useful for responsive card collections and flexible navigation systems.
`flex-grow` determines how a flex item receives positive free space.
When positive free space is available and other constraints permit, the second item receives twice the grow factor of the first.
It does not guarantee an exact final width because the complete flex sizing algorithm considers base sizes, constraints, and available space.
`flex-shrink` controls how flex items shrink when their hypothetical sizes exceed available space.
The sidebar resists shrinking, while the content area can shrink.
The default value of `flex-shrink` is generally 1.
`flex-basis` defines the initial main size used by the flex sizing algorithm.
This provides a starting main size before available space is distributed.
It can be more appropriate than directly using width when building flexible components.
Understand the shorthand rather than copying it without knowing how the sizing algorithm behaves.
The `gap` property controls spacing between flex items.
It avoids managing spacing through individual margins.

sections.title: LESSON 05 — CSS Grid and Two-Dimensional Layouts

blocks.text: CSS Grid is a two-dimensional CSS layout system.
It allows developers to control rows and columns simultaneously.
Flexbox is primarily designed for one-dimensional layouts.
Grid is particularly useful when a layout requires coordinated control over both horizontal and vertical structure.
The direct children of the container become grid items.
Grid organizes content through horizontal and vertical tracks.
A column is a vertical track.
A row is a horizontal track.
The `fr` unit represents a fraction of the available space in the grid track sizing algorithm.
The `fr` unit distributes available grid space proportionally.
When free space is available, the second track receives twice the flexible share of the first.
However, minimum track sizing and content constraints can affect the actual dimensions.
This creates three flexible columns that can shrink within a zero minimum track constraint.
The `repeat()` function reduces repetitive track declarations.
It is particularly useful for repeated layouts.
The `gap` property defines spacing between grid tracks.
Separate row and column gaps can also be configured:
Named grid areas make complex page layouts easier to understand.

Header
Sidebar
Main Content
Footer
Grid areas make layout relationships readable and maintainable.
The assigned grid areas do not change the DOM reading order or keyboard focus order. Keep the source structure meaningful.
Grid items can span across multiple tracks.
This allows an item to occupy two columns.
You can also define explicit grid lines:
This places the item between grid lines 1 and 3.
Grid automatically places items into available grid cells.
As more child elements are added, the browser automatically creates rows when necessary.
This behavior is useful for repeated course and product cards.

These functions are useful for creating responsive repeating track patterns.

This distinction can affect spacing and item width.

The first track has a minimum of 200px and can grow flexibly.
The second track receives a larger flexible share, subject to the grid sizing algorithm.
Grid supports alignment at both container and item levels.
This centers grid items along both alignment axes within their grid areas.
Grid track sizing supports intrinsic sizing concepts.
Represents an intrinsic minimum size based on content wrapping opportunities.
Represents an intrinsic maximum size based on content without soft wrapping constraints.
Allows a track or box to fit available space subject to specified sizing constraints.
These sizing techniques are valuable when building layouts that respond to content rather than relying entirely on fixed measurements.
This creates flexible course columns that adapt according to available width.
The number of columns changes automatically as the available space changes.
| Main use             | Rows or columns                 | Rows and columns            |
| Content distribution | Flexible item sizing            | Track-based layout          |
| Alignment            | Main and cross axes             | Both grid axes              |
| Best for             | Navigation and component groups | Dashboards and page layouts |
| Complex placement    | More limited                    | More powerful               |
They are complementary, not competing technologies.

sections.title: LESSON 06 — Responsive Units, Functions and Custom Properties

blocks.text: Users access websites through different devices and viewport sizes.
A layout designed only for one screen size may become difficult to use on other devices.
Responsive CSS allows interfaces to adapt to available space and user preferences.
The goal is to build interfaces that work across different conditions without maintaining entirely separate designs for every screen size.
Absolute units represent fixed measurements relative to CSS's standardized unit system.
The most commonly used absolute CSS unit is `px`.
CSS pixels are reference pixels, not necessarily the same as one physical hardware pixel.
These are more commonly encountered in print-oriented styling and specialized applications.
Relative units depend on another size or environmental measurement.
Understanding relative units is essential for responsive layout engineering.
Percentages are calculated relative to a property-specific reference.
This width is calculated relative to the relevant containing block.

items: Width percentages commonly depend on the containing block's width.
Height percentages may require a suitable definite containing-block height.
Transform percentages are often relative to the transformed element's own reference box.

blocks.text: Do not assume every percentage uses the same reference dimension.
The `em` unit depends on the element's computed font size for many properties.
For font-size declarations themselves, `em` is relative to the inherited font size.
Nested font-size declarations using `em` can compound.
This makes `em` useful for components whose dimensions should scale with their typography, but it requires care in deeply nested structures.
It is based on the computed font size of the root element.
Unlike `em`, nested `rem` values do not compound through parent font sizes.
This makes rem useful for consistent spacing and type scales.
Viewport units are based on the viewport dimensions.

items: `vw`: 1% of the large viewport width reference used by the unit.
`vh`: 1% of the large viewport height reference.
`vi`: 1% of the viewport's logical inline dimension.
`vb`: 1% of the viewport's logical block dimension.

blocks.text: Dynamic and small viewport variants also exist.
`dvh` responds to dynamic viewport changes, such as browser interface expansion and collapse on mobile devices.
These units help handle modern mobile browser viewport behavior more accurately than relying exclusively on traditional `vh`.
The `ch` unit is based on the advance measure of the zero character in the element's font.
It is frequently used to constrain text width.
This can help create readable line lengths.
It is not exactly equal to an average character width.
The `lh` unit is based on the element's computed line height.
It can help create spacing related to the current text rhythm.

Performs calculations using compatible CSS values.

Selects the largest value among the supplied expressions.
Defines a minimum, preferred, and maximum value.
The browser calculates a value that stays within the defined limits.
This is particularly useful for fluid typography and responsive spacing.
A fixed title size may look appropriate on a desktop but too large on mobile.
The values adapt to viewport width while respecting minimum and maximum sizes.
Always test the intermediate sizes and ensure the text remains readable.
Custom properties allow developers to define reusable values inside stylesheets.
They are commonly called CSS variables.
A fallback can be specified when a custom property is missing or invalid for the consuming declaration.
If `--text-color` cannot provide a usable value, the browser uses the fallback.
A fallback does not automatically replace a declared but unsuitable value in every situation; invalid-at-computed-value behavior must also be understood.
Custom properties generally inherit through the element tree.

An element outside the course card inherits the root-level orange value.
This allows developers to define global design tokens and local component overrides.
Media queries apply CSS conditionally based on the environment.
This provides different layouts at different viewport widths.
Mobile-first development begins with styles suitable for smaller screens.
Then additional layout capabilities are introduced for wider viewports.
Mobile-first is a useful approach, but it is not the only valid responsive strategy. Breakpoints should be selected based on content requirements rather than arbitrary device names.
Media queries generally respond to the viewport or device environment.
Container queries allow a component to adapt according to the size of its containing element.
This is valuable when reusable components appear inside containers of different sizes.
A card can adapt to the space available to it rather than assuming that the complete viewport determines its layout.
Users may configure their operating systems to reduce motion.
This is a starting example, not a universal rule to indiscriminately eliminate every transition.
The application should preserve essential information and functionality while reducing unnecessary motion.
A design token system centralizes repeated design decisions.
This makes it easier to maintain visual consistency across pages and components.

sections.title: LESSON 08 — Pseudo-Classes, Pseudo-Elements and Advanced Selectors

blocks.text: Pseudo-classes allow CSS to target elements based on their state, position, or relationship to other elements.
They begin with a single colon.
This targets a button when it is in the hover state.
Pseudo-classes are useful for interactive styling without requiring additional JavaScript for every visual state.
`:hover` applies when a pointing device is positioned over an element.
Hover should not be the only way users can discover functionality.
Touchscreens and keyboard users may not experience hover in the same way.
`:active` applies while an element is being activated.
It can provide immediate interaction feedback.
`:focus` targets an element when it receives focus.
Focus styling is essential for keyboard navigation.
`:focus-visible` allows developers to provide focus indicators under browser focus-visible heuristics.
It is often useful for accessible keyboard navigation without forcing identical visual focus treatment for every pointer interaction.
Do not remove visible focus indicators without providing an accessible replacement.
Browsers restrict certain styling and information exposure for visited links to protect users' privacy.
Structural pseudo-classes target elements according to their relationships and positions.
Targets an element only when it is the first child of its parent.
Targets the second paragraph among siblings of the same element type.
A common mistake is assuming `nth-child()` counts only matching element types. It counts sibling positions, while `nth-of-type()` filters by element type.
`:empty` selects elements that have no children.

sections.title: LESSON 09 — Transitions, Transforms and CSS Animations

blocks.text: CSS provides several mechanisms for visual motion.
These features allow developers to add interaction feedback, movement, emphasis, and visual storytelling.
Motion should improve usability rather than distract users.
Transitions allow CSS property changes to occur over time.
Instead of switching instantly, the browser gradually interpolates the background color.
Defines how long the transition takes.
Defines how long the browser waits before starting the transition.
Custom timing curves can be created using `cubic-bezier()`.
An appropriate easing curve makes motion feel more natural.
The `transform` property changes an element's visual coordinate transformation without changing its normal-flow position in the same manner as changing layout dimensions.
This visually moves the card upward.
Moves the element along the horizontal axis in the usual coordinate system.
Scaling does not automatically reserve additional layout space, so larger elements may overlap neighboring content.
Rotates the element around its transformation origin.
`transform-origin` controls the origin used for transformations.
Other possible values include corner positions and custom coordinates.
The order of transform functions matters because transformation operations are not generally interchangeable.
Transitions depend on changes between CSS states.
CSS animations can run using predefined keyframes without needing a hover or state change to trigger each intermediate step.
The `@keyframes` rule defines the animation stages.
An animation can contain multiple keyframe percentages.
This plays the animation in alternating directions.
`animation-fill-mode` controls how styles are applied before or after an animation.
The final keyframe styles remain applied after the animation completes.
Infinite animations are useful for loading indicators, but avoid unnecessary continuous motion.
Some animated properties require more rendering work than others.

sections.title: LESSON 10 — CSS Architecture, Naming Conventions and Maintainability

blocks.text: Small projects may begin with a single stylesheet containing a few rules.
As an application grows, CSS can become difficult to maintain.
CSS architecture defines how styles are organized, named, reused, and maintained.
The objective is to make styling predictable across large projects and teams.
Global CSS establishes shared project-wide behavior.
Component styles describe the appearance of specific interface components.
A good architecture defines which styles should be global and which should belong to individual components.
Naming conventions make styles easier to understand.
Use names that communicate component purpose rather than temporary appearance.
BEM stands for Block, Element, Modifier.
It provides a naming convention for organizing component-related styles.
Represents a part of the block.
Represents a variation in state or appearance.

Frontend Engineering

Learn modern frontend development.

Explore Course
BEM is not a CSS feature. It is a naming methodology used by development teams.
Utility classes describe small, reusable styling operations.
However, excessive utility-class combinations can make markup difficult to understand if the project lacks conventions.
Design tokens are named values representing reusable design decisions.
Tokens allow teams to update shared values without manually editing many unrelated components.

styles/
│
├── reset.css
├── tokens.css
├── typography.css
├── base.css
├── layout.css
├── components/

│   └── course-card.css
│
├── pages/
│   ├── home.css
│   └── courses.css
│
└── utilities.css
The structure should match the size and complexity of the project.
There is no universally correct folder structure.
ITCSS stands for Inverted Triangle CSS.
It is an architectural approach that organizes styles from broad and low-specificity rules toward more specific component and utility rules.
The principle is to manage specificity and scope as the stylesheet becomes more specific.
ITCSS is an organizational methodology, not part of the CSS language.
A large stylesheet becomes difficult to maintain when every new feature requires a more specific selector.
You can also use cascade layers:
This makes the stylesheet's intended precedence easier to reason about.
CSS custom properties can implement themes.
The application can change the `data-theme` attribute to switch themes.
A full theme system must also account for forms, controls, focus indicators, borders, and other interface states.

The goal is not to create the largest architecture possible. It is to introduce only the structure required to keep the application maintainable.

sections.title: LESSON 11 — CSS Modules and Component-Level Styling

blocks.text: CSS Modules are a component-oriented CSS styling approach used with frontend build systems.
They allow developers to write normal CSS while providing locally scoped class names through build-time processing.
The `.title` class is globally available to matching elements in the document.
If several components use `.title`, their styles can unintentionally affect one another.
CSS Modules help prevent this problem by generating locally scoped class identifiers.
CSS Modules are not a native browser CSS feature.
They are implemented through tooling such as Vite, webpack, and compatible framework integrations.
Consider a large frontend application containing:
Without a styling strategy, classes may become difficult to coordinate.
A class with the same name may be used in multiple unrelated components.
Changes intended for one component could accidentally alter another.
CSS Modules help isolate component-specific class names.
The `.module.css` suffix tells a compatible build system to process the stylesheet as a CSS Module.
The class definitions are exported as a mapping to generated class names.
The imported `styles` object provides access to the processed class names.
The original CSS class names are mapped to generated identifiers.
Suppose two components define a class named `.title`.
Although the source class names are identical, the build system generates distinct scoped identifiers for each module.
This prevents accidental class-name collisions under normal CSS Modules processing.
A component may need multiple styles.
The component receives both scoped classes.
Conditional classes can also be applied based on application state.
CSS Modules supports class composition in compatible implementations.
Composition support and syntax can depend on the CSS Modules implementation and configured build tooling.
Another option is to reuse custom properties and shared global utility classes.
Do not assume every ordinary CSS feature or build-tool extension works identically in every CSS Modules integration.
Some global styles still need to be shared.
With compatible CSS Modules tooling, `:global()` can be used to target global classes or selectors.
Keep global styles intentional and centralized.
Do not turn every CSS Module into a global stylesheet.
CSS Modules work with standard CSS custom properties.
The global design tokens may be defined in a shared stylesheet:
This combines local class isolation with shared design-system values.
| Class scope          | Global by default             | Locally scoped                 |
| Shared styles        | Directly available            | Imported or explicitly shared  |
| Build tooling        | Not always required           | Usually requires tooling       |
| Component isolation  | Must be managed manually      | Supported by module processing |
| Global design tokens | Straightforward               | Can use shared CSS files       |
| Best use             | Resets and design foundations | Component-specific styling     |
Most production applications benefit from a combination of shared global styles and local component styling.
CSS Modules and CSS-in-JS are different styling approaches.

After completing this module, students should be capable of translating a visual design into a responsive, maintainable CSS implementation.
They should understand how the browser resolves styles, how layout systems distribute space, how positioning and stacking contexts work, and how responsive interfaces adapt to different screen sizes.

They should also be able to establish reusable design tokens, manage typography, implement interaction states, create performant animations, and organize styles for large component-based applications.

The expected outcome is not simply the ability to make HTML elements look attractive. It is the ability to engineer reliable visual systems that can be maintained and extended as a real frontend application grows.
